clue.text: Marvellous boy, Wordsworth, to make foolish talk the fashion

parts.note: idle prattle or gabble
'the ton' is an old word for high fashion or society

explanation.surface: Wordsworth is asked to turn idle gossip into the latest craze.
explanation.walkthrough: Wordsworth called the boy-poet who died at seventeen 'the marvellous Boy' in 'Resolution and Independence', so the name of the poet is the definition, attributed to Wordsworth.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Chatterton, the teenage forger-poet, is the youth Wordsworth's poem praises with that phrase.

clue.text: It helps to varnish many a gem

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a crossword stand-in for 'many'
an opal is an iridescent gemstone

explanation.surface: A jeweller's tip that varnish brings out the shine of plenty of stones.
explanation.definitionFit: Copal is a tree resin dissolved to make clear varnishes, so it is an ingredient that helps varnish.

clue.text: Add years of experience as a hanger-on

parts.note: to append is to add on at the end
age is the years one has lived, bringing experience

explanation.surface: Someone with a long CV is dismissed as a mere hanger-on.
explanation.definitionFit: An appendage is something attached that dangles from a larger body, literally or figuratively a dependant.

clue.text: Boswell's dedication to subject of TV?

definitions.text: Boswell's dedication to subject of TV?

parts.words: Boswell's dedication to subject of TV?
parts.note: Boswell wrote the Life of Johnson, so his dedication to his subject would announce the biography; the same words were the famous catchphrase of a TV programme surprising a guest with their life story

explanation.surface: A biographer's inscription doubles as a television catchphrase.
explanation.walkthrough: The surprise TV show presented its guest with a big red book of their life; Boswell, presenting his biography to Johnson, could have said the same words.
explanation.definitionFit: A biographer handing over the book would tell the subject the volume tells their story, the phrase the TV host used.

clue.text: Sapper fit to make a comeback we hear

parts.note: RE, the Royal Engineers, whose soldiers are sappers
sound means healthy, in good condition

explanation.surface: A recovered army engineer gets ready to return to action, so people say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we hear' is not a homophone signal: it belongs to the definition, since a noise that rings back is a comeback you hear.
explanation.definitionFit: To echo or ring out again is a returning noise that the listener hears.

clue.text: One's peculiar quality ?

parts.note: read as the quality belonging to the number one, it is being an odd, not even, number; read normally it is strangeness

explanation.surface: A question about what makes somebody distinctive.
explanation.definitionFit: Strangeness is a peculiar quality, and the number one's own property is not being even.

clue.text: Ignited by ambitious Oxonians ?

parts.note: the Oxford stretch of the Thames is the river on which ambitious Oxford rowers race, so they 'set it on fire'

explanation.surface: Ambitious Oxford students set something alight.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'set the Thames on fire' is to do something remarkable; at Oxford the Thames is called by another name, so ambitious undergraduates would set that river alight.
explanation.definitionFit: Oxford's name for the upper Thames is the river whose figurative burning the clue alludes to.

clue.text: Is this a dagger ?" Point taken by Shakespearian actor

indicators.note: the compass point is taken on by the actor, so it stands joined at his front

parts.note: S, south, is one of the compass points
Edmund Kean, the great Regency actor of Shakespeare

explanation.surface: Macbeth's famous line, and an actor seizes the point of it.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition quotes Macbeth's dagger speech; the answer is a Gaelic dagger, as in the Highland skean-dhu.
explanation.definitionFit: A skean is a short Scottish or Irish knife, so it is the sort of weapon the question asks about.

clue.text: One thing Churchill's beach fighters would never do

definitions.text: One thing Churchill's beach fighters would never do

parts.words: One thing Churchill's beach fighters would never do
parts.note: recalls the 1940 speech 'we shall fight on the beaches ... we shall never' give in

explanation.surface: A reminder of Churchill's wartime speech about fighting on the beaches.
explanation.definitionFit: The speech ends by vowing never to yield, the act of giving oneself up to the enemy.

clue.text: It might dawn on Jock during the night

definitions.text: It might dawn on Jock during the night

parts.words: It might dawn on Jock during the night
parts.note: a Scot in the far north might see a night-time light named after the dawn goddess and the north wind

explanation.surface: A Scotsman has a sudden realisation in the night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jock' is a nickname for a Scot; 'dawn on' looks like 'occur to', but Aurora is the dawn goddess and the northern lights are seen in Scotland at night.
explanation.definitionFit: The northern lights are a glow in the night sky named after a dawn goddess, best seen from northern latitudes like Scotland.

clue.text: Popular birds to do Rosemary's job in November

definitions.text: to do Rosemary's job in November

parts.note: pop is short for popular
pies are magpies, an old name for the bird

explanation.surface: Well-liked birds take over a woman's work in the autumn.
explanation.walkthrough: Rosemary is not a woman: Ophelia's 'rosemary, that's for remembrance'; red flowers do the job of remembrance on Remembrance Day in November.
explanation.definitionFit: Red paper flowers are worn in November as the emblem of remembrance, a role rosemary traditionally plays.

clue.text: Soppy thing, French !

parts.note: a sop is a bribe or gratuity given to appease, and the word for such a tip borrowed from French means sweetness

explanation.surface: Someone mocks a sentimental Frenchman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soppy' looks like 'sentimental', but here it means 'serving as a sop', a little bribe to keep someone sweet.
explanation.definitionFit: A tip or bribe is a sop, and the French loan word for such a sweetener is the answer.

clue.text: Its lines run between poles

parts.note: suggests telegraph wires on poles, but means meridians on a globe running from North to South Pole

explanation.surface: Something whose cables are strung from post to post.
explanation.definitionFit: Meridians, the lines measuring east-west position, all run from the North Pole to the South.

clue.text: In short it would be a wizard home — for a cat

definitions.text: In short it would be a wizard home
definitions.meaning: the abbreviation of this unit of weight is OZ, the land of the Wizard of Oz
the snow leopard of Central Asia

explanation.surface: Abbreviated, it is a magician's homeland; in full, a big cat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In short' means 'abbreviated': the weight's abbreviation OZ names the Wizard's land.
explanation.definitionFit: The snow leopard is also called by this name, and the same word as a weight is shortened to OZ, the Wizard's country.

clue.text: As cautious as Mrs Mopp?

parts.note: Mrs Mopp was the charlady of the radio show ITMA, so 'like a char' would be ...-..., a word meaning wary

explanation.surface: A comparison with a famous comic cleaner.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Mopp was the cleaning lady in the wartime BBC radio comedy ITMA; a char is a cleaning woman, and adding -Y makes a word for wary.
explanation.definitionFit: Being wary and reluctant to take risks is cautious, and the word looks like 'char-like'.

clue.text: One qualified for an Olympian pub career perhaps?

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters of the phrase might be arranged differently

explanation.surface: Someone suited to a top-level career running a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges PUBCAREER; Ganymede and Hebe poured nectar for the gods on Olympus, so the server qualifies as an Olympian's attendant.
explanation.definitionFit: The gods on Olympus had a servant to pour their wine, a role filled by Ganymede and Hebe.

clue.text: Threw away record publicity about mad Eric the Explorer

parts.note: a disc is a gramophone record

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the advertisement wraps round the scrambled explorer

parts.note: an ad, advertisement, is publicity

indicators.note: mad suggests the letters of the explorer's name are crazily jumbled

parts.note: Eric the Red, the Norse explorer who settled Greenland

explanation.surface: Someone throws out the publicity record of a crazy Viking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eric the Explorer' is not an anagram of Eric: it is the Viking Eric the Red, and only his nickname is scrambled by 'mad' before 'about' wraps the advertisement round it.
explanation.definitionFit: To throw something away is to get rid of it as no longer wanted.

clue.text: Mike's hidden, after rough drawing of Hitler's weapon

indicators.note: after places the hidden microphone behind the sketch

parts.note: a doodle is an idle scribble
a hidden mike, a concealed microphone, is a bug

explanation.surface: A microphone is concealed after a sketch of a Nazi weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mike' looks like a name, but is a microphone.
explanation.definitionFit: The V-1 flying bomb Germany fired at London was nicknamed this by Londoners.

clue.text: Taking liberty, like Stanley at Ujiji

definitions.meaning: being forward, taking too much for granted
Stanley greeted Livingstone at Ujiji with 'Dr Livingstone, I presume?'

explanation.surface: The explorer takes a liberty on meeting Livingstone.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry Morton Stanley found David Livingstone at Ujiji, on Lake Tanganyika, in 1871 and asked whether he was the doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking things for granted is being forward, and Stanley at Ujiji was famously supposing he had met Livingstone.

clue.text: Heap coals of fire here, by you thanking him

definitions.meaning: read literally, a coal fire is piled up in the fireplace
to 'heap coals of fire on his head' is to repay an ungrateful person with kindness, as by thanking him

explanation.surface: A biblical saying about repaying the unthankful with kindness.
explanation.walkthrough: Proverbs and Romans say returning good for evil 'heaps coals of fire' on someone's head; literally, coals are heaped in a grate, which is how the answer splits.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who shows no gratitude is the person on whose head kindness heaps coals, and coals go into a fireplace grate.

clue.text: Spanish Noble, the horse, simply eats money in S Africa

indicators.note: eats means the horse takes the money inside itself

parts.note: gee or gee-gee is a childish or simple word for a horse
the rand is South Africa's currency

explanation.surface: A Spanish aristocrat's horse lives on cash in South Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: A Spanish nobleman of the highest rank is a grandee.

clue.text: If it's bad, Stinker's bound to be in it

definitions.text: If it's bad, Stinker's bound to be in it

parts.words: If it's bad, Stinker's bound to be in it
parts.note: to be 'in bad' smell is to be out of favour, and a stinker would naturally be in a bad smell

explanation.surface: Whenever there is trouble, the rotter is sure to be mixed up in it.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'stinker' is a nasty person; being in bad odour means being in disgrace, and literally a stinker carries a smell.
explanation.definitionFit: A smell is what a stinker gives off, and being in a bad one means disgrace.

clue.text: Peer being more so ?

parts.note: a peer is one's match; Orwell's Animal Farm has some animals 'more ... than others'

explanation.surface: A question about a nobleman becoming even grander.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peer' suggests a lord, but means an equal; Orwell's pigs claimed to be more so than the other animals.
explanation.definitionFit: A peer is someone of the same standing, and Orwell's pigs were more of that than the rest.

clue.text: Free demonstration in Home Counties

indicators.note: the letters are demonstrated, put on show, within the words that follow

explanation.surface: An open-air protest in the counties around London.
explanation.walkthrough: The Home Counties are the counties surrounding London; the letters sit inside 'Counties'.
explanation.definitionFit: To free something is to undo the knot holding it.

clue.text: Perplexed by serious local depression coming back

parts.note: grave means serious

indicators.note: coming back means the hollow's name is read in reverse

parts.note: a dell is a small wooded hollow, a dialect or local word

explanation.surface: A local slump in the economy leaves someone baffled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming back' reverses DELL to LLED.
explanation.definitionFit: To be gravelled is an old term for being nonplussed or stuck, as if run aground on gravel.

clue.text: A "dangerous thing" in the underworld for music-makers

annotationWithheld.clue: A "dangerous thing" in the underworld for music-makers

clue.text: A Kipling poem by a sailor -all in return for a liqueur

indicators.note: says the whole string of pieces is then read backwards

parts.note: 'If—' is Kipling's famous poem
a tar is a sailor

explanation.surface: A Kipling verse and a seaman lead, all round, to a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all in return' reverses the whole run A IF A TAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Ratafia is an almond-flavoured liqueur or cordial.

clue.text: Considers loss of rate — for his job on Coppélia?

definitions.note: a person, named for the work he did on the ballet

indicators.note: loss of means the named word is removed from the longer one

parts.note: deliberates means considers or ponders
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone weighs the loss of a rate rise against their work on a ballet.
explanation.walkthrough: Coppélia is a ballet, and Léo Delibes wrote its music, so the man is defined by his job.
explanation.definitionFit: Léo Delibes was the French composer who wrote the score for the ballet.

clue.text: Smoke of old Edinburgh

parts.note: Edinburgh's nickname 'Auld ..., Old Smoky, comes from the Scots word for smoke

explanation.surface: The haze that hung over Edinburgh in the past.
explanation.walkthrough: Edinburgh was called Auld Reekie for its chimney smoke; the Scots word for smoke gives the name.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots the word for smoke gave Edinburgh its nickname Auld Reekie.

clue.text: Classic brains show man's acts are without point

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the acts surround the point

parts.note: in As You Like It, 'one man in his time plays many parts, his acts being seven ages'
S, south, a compass point

explanation.surface: Clever people demonstrate that human deeds are pointless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' means 'outside': the seven ages of Jaques' speech enclose S, the point, to give the Seven Sages of ancient Greece.
explanation.definitionFit: The Seven Sages were the seven wise men of ancient Greece, such as Solon and Thales.
